messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 70
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Photographer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 75

# Margaret's Careful Eye

Margaret sits in the studio she's built over forty years, surrounded by the work that has defined her life. At seventy, she still moves through her darkroom with practiced precision, though her hands shake more than they used to. The photographs on her walls—landscapes mostly, a few portraits—testify to a woman who learned early to see the world through a lens, to frame it, to control it.

She was eight when her father's drinking worsened. Margaret's mother had already retreated into silence, the way she did with most things. Her father's hands, which had once helped her build things in the garage, became unpredictable. A wrong word at dinner. A plate cleared too slowly. His belt came off without warning. Margaret learned to read the small signs—the particular way he poured his drink, the set of his jaw—and to make herself small. She would hide in the garden shed, peering through cracks in the wood, watching the world in fragments. This became her first camera: a way to observe without being seen, to exist safely in the space between herself and everything else.

The photography came naturally. By her twenties, Margaret had built a reputation for her ability to capture something true in people's faces, a vulnerability they didn't know they'd shown. She worked constantly, taking on assignments, building her business. She married briefly—a kind man who wanted more of her attention than she could give—and divorced after seven years. The camera was easier. The camera didn't ask for presence in the way people did.

Now, at seventy, Margaret cannot explain why certain sounds still send her body into revolt. A door slamming. A man's raised voice, even on a television show she's trying to watch. Her heart races and her hands go numb, and she finds herself standing in her bathroom without remembering how she got there. Last month, a young male client raised his voice in frustration during a portrait session—nothing directed at her, just impatience with the lighting—and Margaret's vision tunneled. She excused herself and locked herself in the darkroom for twenty minutes, her breath shallow, convinced something terrible was about to happen.

She doesn't sleep well. She lies in bed at three in the morning, her mind rehearsing old conversations, old moments of helplessness. Sometimes she wakes already standing, having no memory of leaving the bed. She keeps her bedroom door locked now, a habit that embarrasses her even as she does it. She's seventy years old, living alone, and yet some part of her is still eight, still waiting for the sound of his footsteps.

The photography has changed too. Margaret used to seek out human connection through her lens, those unguarded moments. Now she finds herself drawn almost exclusively to landscapes—empty beaches, mountains, forests where no one is watching and nothing can hurt her. Her recent work is technically flawless but emotionally distant. A gallery owner who's shown her work for decades asked gently if everything was all right. Margaret couldn't answer.

She recognizes that she's become more isolated. The few friendships she's maintained have thinned from her own withdrawal. She cancels plans. She avoids situations where she can't control the environment. The rational part of her mind—the part that has built a successful career and lived an independent life—watches this pattern with frustration. But the other part, the part that never really left that garden shed, keeps her vigilant, keeps her small, keeps her safe.
